issues.legal_issue: A bill passed by a provincial legislative chamber and awaiting assent when the Constitution commenced could be continued by the corresponding State legislature.
material_facts: The provincial assembly passed the acquisition bill and it was reserved for consideration by the Governor-General.
The Governor-General returned the bill to the Governor with a suggestion that it be reserved for the President, and the bill was in transit when the Constitution commenced.
The Governor-General neither assented to the bill nor expressly withheld assent, and his suggestion showed an intention that it remain pending.
After the Constitution commenced, the Governor reserved the bill for the President; the State assembly considered proposed alterations, passed the amended bill, and the President assented to it.
issues.conclusion: The bill remained pending before the provincial legislature when the Constitution commenced and was validly continued and enacted by the corresponding State legislature.
issues.legal_principle: Article 389 keeps alive a bill pending in the predecessor legislature and permits its continuation by the corresponding State legislature. Under sections 18, 60, 75 and 76 of the Government of India Act, 1935, the Governor or Governor-General represented the sovereign, who formed part of the legislature; a bill presented for assent remained pending until assent was given or withheld. The meaning of “Legislature” depends on context and, in Article 389, includes the machinery involved in the entire legislative process. A suggestion to reserve a bill for further consideration, without a positive declaration withholding assent, does not terminate it. The Court distinguished the broader contextual reading from the passage in Visweshwar Rao v. The State of Madhya Pradesh, [1952] S.C.R. 1020.

rule.if: constitutional_validity_challenge and predecessor_chamber_passed_bill and bill_awaited_assent_at_constitutional_transition and assent_not_expressly_withheld

predicates.constitutional_validity_challenge: A party challenged the validity of a law on the ground that its enactment process was defective.
predicates.predecessor_chamber_passed_bill: The predecessor legislature's chamber passed the bill before the constitutional transition.
predicates.bill_awaited_assent_at_constitutional_tr: The bill had reached the assent stage and remained unresolved when the constitutional transition occurred.
predicates.assent_not_expressly_withheld: The authority considering the bill did not expressly withhold assent and instead indicated that further consideration was intended.

issues.definition: When a validity challenge concerns a bill passed by the predecessor chamber that remained awaiting assent at the constitutional transition, and assent was not expressly withheld, the bill may be continued and enacted by the successor legislature.

issues.legal_issue: A compulsory-acquisition bill was not invalid for want of prior executive sanction where the record showed that sanction had been given and the law also barred invalidation solely on that ground.
material_facts: The bill provided for compulsory acquisition of land and therefore required prior sanction before its introduction under the law then in force.
An official departmental file placed the request for sanction before the Governor, whose initials appeared on the file after the request.
The Court found that the initials signified the Governor's sanction, although the words “sanction granted” were not written on the file.
issues.conclusion: The bill was not invalid for want of prior sanction; in any event, the statute could not be challenged as invalid solely because prior sanction had not been given.
issues.legal_principle: Section 299(3) of the Government of India Act, 1935 required the Governor's previous sanction for introducing a provincial bill providing for transfer of land to public ownership. The record showed that sanction had been given. Section 109 also prevented the enacted law from being challenged as invalid merely because prior sanction had not been given. These provisions were applied in the context of a challenge to the validity of the acquisition law.

predicates.constitutional_validity_challenge: A party challenged the validity of an enacted law on the ground of a defect in its enactment process.
predicates.compulsory_land_acquisition_bill: The bill provided for compulsory acquisition of land for public ownership.
predicates.governor_sanction_recorded_before_introd: The official record showed that the Governor had approved the bill before it was introduced.

issues.definition: In a challenge to an acquisition law, where the bill provided for compulsory land acquisition and the record shows the Governor's prior approval, the law is not invalid for want of prior sanction.

issues.legal_issue: A law providing for State acquisition of estates, after receiving the President's assent, is protected from challenge based on rights in Part III of the Constitution.
material_facts: The challenged law authorized the State to acquire estates or tenures and provided for their transfer to the State free from encumbrances.
The law defined estates by reference to land entries in general registers maintained under the land-tenure law, and the properties of the parties were entered in those registers.
The law had been reserved for the President and received the President's assent.
issues.conclusion: The law provided for State acquisition of estates and was protected by Article 31-A, so its validity could not be challenged for contravening rights in Part III, including property rights and equality rights.
issues.legal_principle: Article 31-A protects a law providing for acquisition by the State of an estate or rights in an estate from challenge for inconsistency with, or taking away or abridging, rights in Part III. Article 31-A(2)(a) gives “estate” the meaning assigned by the existing land-tenure law for the relevant area. The Court also explained that Article 31-A affords wider protection than Article 31(4), which concerns only Article 31(2), and that the President's assent meant the proviso to Article 31-A did not apply.

predicates.constitutional_validity_challenge: A party challenged the validity of a law by alleging that it infringed constitutional rights.
predicates.law_provides_state_acquisition_of_estate: The law provides for the State to acquire estates or rights in estates as understood under the applicable land-tenure law.
predicates.presidential_assent_given: The President assented to the law.

issues.definition: A law challenged on constitutional-rights grounds is protected from a Part III rights challenge when it provides for State acquisition of estates and received the President's assent.

issues.legal_issue: A complaint that the compensation fixed by an estate-acquisition law is illusory cannot be recast as a colourable exercise of legislative power when legislative competence is not in issue and the law is protected by Article 31-A.
material_facts: The appellants argued that the compensation provisions produced illusory or no compensation and therefore constituted a colourable exercise of legislative power.
The Court found no question of legislative incompetence and treated the complaint as one about the quantum of compensation.
The Court had concluded that the law was protected by Article 31-A.
issues.conclusion: The compensation complaint could not invalidate the law as a colourable exercise of legislative power, and the quantum of compensation could not be challenged in view of Article 31-A.
issues.legal_principle: The doctrine of colourable legislation concerns legislative competence; it does not provide a basis to challenge the amount of compensation where competence is not in issue. Under Article 31-A, a complaint relating to the quantum of compensation for an acquisition protected by that article is barred. The Court relied on K. C. Gajapati Narain Deb v. State of Orissa, [1954] S.C.R. 1.

rule.if: constitutional_validity_challenge and estate_acquisition_law_protected_from_rights_challenge and compensation_amount_is_complaint and legislative_competence_not_in_issue

predicates.constitutional_validity_challenge: A party challenged the validity of an enacted law.
predicates.estate_acquisition_law_protected_from_ri: The challenged law provides for acquisition of estates and is protected from a Part III rights challenge.
predicates.compensation_amount_is_complaint: The party's complaint concerns the amount or adequacy of compensation provided for the acquisition.
predicates.legislative_competence_not_in_issue: The challenge does not allege that the legislature lacked authority to enact the law.

issues.definition: When a challenge to a protected estate-acquisition law concerns compensation adequacy rather than legislative authority, the law cannot be invalidated as a colourable exercise on that basis.

issues.legal_issue: The classifications and selective coverage in the acquisition law did not amount to discrimination between estates or proprietors.
material_facts: The appellants argued that the State could select some estates for acquisition while leaving others untouched.
The law covered Lakheraj estates within permanently settled areas but not other Lakheraj estates; the former were treated as a distinct class whose acquisition furthered the law's object.
The law prescribed different compensation scales for proprietors in different income groups, for which the Court found a rational basis.
The Court also held that Article 31-A independently prevented a challenge to the law under Part III.
issues.conclusion: The law did not violate equality by permitting selection of estates, limiting coverage to Lakheraj estates within permanently settled areas, or prescribing different compensation scales for different income groups.
issues.legal_principle: Article 31-A protects qualifying estate-acquisition laws from challenges under Part III. Independently, Article 14 permits classifications with a rational basis: Lakheraj estates within permanently settled areas formed a distinct class, and different compensation scales for proprietors in different income groups had a rational basis. The Court relied on Biswambhar Singh v. The State of Orissa, [1954] S.C.R. 842, and Thakur Amar Singh v. The State of Rajasthan, [1955] 2 S.C.R. 303.

rule.if: constitutional_validity_challenge and estate_acquisition_law and acquisition_categories_have_rational_basis and compensation_groups_have_rational_basis

predicates.constitutional_validity_challenge: A party challenged the validity of a law on constitutional equality grounds.
predicates.estate_acquisition_law: The challenged law provides for State acquisition of estates.
predicates.acquisition_categories_have_rational_bas: The categories of estates selected for acquisition are distinct and their selection furthers the law's object.
predicates.compensation_groups_have_rational_basis: Different compensation treatment is based on rationally distinct groups, such as proprietors in different income groups.

issues.definition: In an equality challenge to an estate-acquisition law, selective coverage and differing compensation treatment are not discriminatory when the acquisition categories and compensation groups each have a rational basis.
